sentences.text: The body of Lepidotes was covered with thick, enamelled scales that were ovular in shape. These robust scales measured 18.5 mm in length and were 3 mm thick at their thickest point.

Woodward identified many characteristics in 1895, including a moderately compressed fusiform trunk, compressed marginal teeth, smooth stouter inner teeth, ossified ribs, very large fin-fulcrums, small paired fins, short deep dorsal and anal fins, robust scales, and inconspicuous dorsal and ventral ridge-scales.

L. elvensis was described by Ducrotay de Blainville in 1818, originally classified as a species of Cyprinus. The type specimen of L. elvensis comes from a Toarcian-aged deposit in La Caine, France, and is housed in the Paris Museum of Natural History.

L. semiserratus was named by Agassiz in 1837 and is known from incomplete remains. L. semiserratus is known from the Upper Lias of Yorkshire, England, specifically the Toarcian-aged Whitby Mudstone Formation.
Based on some specimens, L. gigas could measure up to 75 cm in length.
Lepidotes could reach a maximum length of 30 centimeters.
Lepidotes was one of the earliest fish where upper jawbones were detached from the jugal bone, allowing jaws to stretch into a 'tube' for sucking prey from a greater distance.
Stomach contents from Early Jurassic Germany suggest Lepidotes fed on soft-bodied prey, grasping it with slender marginal teeth and crushing it with rounded palatal teeth.
Lepidotes inhabited both shallow seas and freshwater bodies and possessed strong teeth used to grind and shred bivalves.
Lepidotes belongs to the clade Ginglymodi, which contains only living representatives in the form of modern gars.
Lepidotes is classified within the family Semionotidae.
Lepidotes was a primitive neopterygian, more advanced than earlier primitive actinopterigians.
The type species L. gigas is known from the Early Jurassic (Toarcian) of Germany, specifically from the Posidonia Shale lagerstätte.
L. semiserratus is known from the Upper Lias of Yorkshire, England, specifically the Toarcian-aged Whitby Mudstone Formation.
Recent arguments suggest restricting Lepidotes to species closely related to L. gigas from the Early Jurassic of Western and Central Europe, transferring others to new genera like Scheenstia.
